title: When Should a Quantity Have Its Own Dimension? — Uniqueness of Natural Units as a Design Criterion
description:
We propose a cross-kind design criterion: for a specified kind of quantity, a numerical value can identify the quantity without an externally supplied reference convention when independent users have a unique natural unit on which to converge. Where two or more comparably natural candidates exist, the number alone leaves the reference unsettled. Assigning the kind a distinct dimension makes distinctions between kinds testable within equations; the choice between units of the same kind is recorded by unit notation or by named, dimensioned conversion constants.

The criterion adjudicates the amount of substance (unique natural unit; the mole legitimate but optional), the plane and solid angles (two incommensurable candidates each; an independent plane-angle dimension and a derived solid-angle dimension recommended), and the baseless logarithm (three candidates, purely mathematical) within a single framework, and reads the documented incoherence between the hertz and the radian per second, and the century-old rationalization controversy in electromagnetism, as consequences of leaving the choice between such candidates implicit.

The paper proposes no change to the SI. It examines the Universal Unit System (UUS) / Harmonic System, which made the opposite design choice, as an existence proof.

Version 1.1 restates the criterion in terms of where a unit system records the reference (unit labels and usage rules, or also the algebra of its quantity equations), distinguishes the two benefits of a distinct dimension, adds Lewis & Coveney (2026) and the 2026 CGPM decision on UTC, and renumbers the references in order of first citation.

This record contains the English version (canonical) and a Japanese translation.
